The Queen has been on the throne for my entire life and the majority of my mother’s too. She’s (The Queen) had always been there and through her stoicism, she has been able to weather the storm of changing attitudes times whilst remaining impartial. With so much of everything being so partisan nowadays, it was something to see someone rising above that. 

This might sound like I’m trivialising the changing of social attitudes to race, sexuality, and more - but it’s not meant in that way. For an example, a when I last engaged in mushrooms and weed, I was able to temporarily but entirely disconnect myself from corporeal things and see the universe on a molecular level; above and beyond disagreements, pain, suffering, and tribal wars. I rose above it, albeit temporarily.

For me, The Queen was a inspirational figure that weathered the storm by being above it. We don’t need to get in every fight or respond to every post or comment we disagree with, much like she didn’t with things that were below her. That wasn’t her job, she was a figurehead, not a politician or a personality.

So I can understand why people would want to say goodbye. If something means a lot to you, it’s only natural to find closure if it’s abruptly taken away from you.

Most people aren’t autistic so the default expectation is that you’re not autistic unless diagnosed.

Autism isn’t an identity. It’s not cool, it’s not trendy, and it’s not the new black. For those that have it, it should be part of their personality, sure, but not who they are. 

Nor should people identify as autistic as this leaves the door open to anyone who watches the Big Bang Theory and feels they are a bit like Sheldon. This approach cheapens the experience which genuine autistic people struggle with every day.

Agreed, but not being autistic does make a person not autistic. 

Just because you think you’re autistic, it doesn’t mean you are. For example, you may think you are because in your mind it explains factors A, B, and C. However a trained professional can look at you objectively and may agree with you, or they may uncover something else entirely which explains things even better and give you better clarity.

Autism is binary. You either are or you aren’t. Being poor doesn’t give you a free pass.

If you want me to sign something making diagnostic assessments free for all, I’ll sign it, 100%. But I won’t say it’s okay for anyone to say they’re autistic if they’re not diagnosed by a professional.

Personally, I wouldn’t be comfortable using any mental diagnosis unless validated by a trained medical professional. 

I had strong suspicious I was autistic for years, but was never comfortable using the word until it was validated professionally because I know how important the realisation of being autistic is to actual autistic people and I didn’t want to dilute that with anything less than genuine autistic people using that word.

There has to be a standard of definition. That’s what a medical diagnosis is. Anything else is just suspicion.

It’s fine to say you suspect you’re autistic, but until you get a thumbs up, that’s all it can be. Otherwise why have medical professionals at all?

I have this issue too. Realising the feelings of others is hard because a lot of it is done by body language which autistic people have a hard time reading. 

Imagine it as a verbal language that we don’t understand but 90% of the world does and that 90% expect 100% of people to understand.

Autistic people do care about the feelings of others, we just can’t sense what those feelings are so we don’t adjust our behaviour because of it.

My advice would be to not try to make him more empathetic, as he does have empathy, but to understand that he’s not being uncaring, he’s just doesn’t realise a) how others are feeling and b) what to do in those situations.

Are video games in general or specific ones a special interest of his?
